newsitem.title: USA: Duval Cty, Fla., to meet Hough on 1992 refinancing.
newsitem.headline: Duval Cty, Fla., to meet Hough on 1992 refinancing.

text.p: School officials in Florida's Duval County will meet "in the near future" with officials from William R Hough & Co to discuss the firm's handling of a 1992 school bond refinancing, a school board attorney said.
Officials at William Hough were unavailable for comment.

Florida Times-Union reported last month that the firm earned $700,000 in profits from U.S. Treasury securities it sold as part of a 1992 school bond refinancing. The newspaper said that was in addition to the $50,000 fee Hough earned as financial adviser on the deal.

The newspaper quoted a Hough official as saying the firm's markup on the Treasuries was substantially lower than $700,000 and that it "was appropriate" given the volatility of the bond market, uncertainty of the deal, and comparable prices charged by other investment firms.
Duval school board attorney Ernst Mueller told Reuters that school board officials planned to meet Hough offcials soon "to review the events."

The newspaper questioned whether the board could be forced to pay back taxes on the bonds, and whether Internal Revenue Service could retroactively declare the bonds taxable under its yield burning enforcement measure.

Yield burning occurs when underwriters overcharge issuers for Treasury securities used in escrow accounts for municipal bond refundings, seemingly complying with federal arbitrage restrictions while creating a windfall for the underwriters.

A June ruling by IRS said issuers can avoid having the interest on their bonds delcared taxable by paying the Treasury the difference between the price they paid and the spot price of the securities on the purchase date, plus interest. The ruling puts the onus on issuers, even if the profit went to investment firms.
But Mueller said, "This whole thing about retro-application of IRS rules, at this point at least, is at best a remote possibility."
He added, "This is a tempest created by the media."

He said the school board had asked Hough for information about the refunding because school officials could not find their records from the five-year-old deal and that officials who handled it were no longer with the district.
"We're sort of in a position of trying to find out, well, what happened back then and what does it mean," Mueller said.

He added, "The firm (Hough) has an excellet reputation. They are regarded as a friendly, completely ethical entity around here. I assume the amicable fiduciary relationship that previously existed (with the school board) will continue."
While yield-burning allegations have prompted three lawsuits in two states, Mueller said the Duval school board had no plans for litigation.
"Certainly there is nothing to sue about that I know of," he said.
